note: Track arpeggios (guitar-caged), step 3: the A minor arpeggio with its 7th added, then A7 and Amaj7 from the same root, then Am7, D7 and Gmaj7 played through in one area of the neck. Each block has a feel to reach, the arpeggio says where it starts and turns, and the tempo is moves (66 to 86 bpm). The chords keep their letters: a chord token counts from the first chord's root (A), so it would number this ii–V–I of G as if it were in A. missing: an arpeggio's boxes are numbered per chord, so a chord-steps or arpeggio-neck set by box can't follow a key move; the block stays in one key.

exercise.title: 7th arpeggios: one more note
exercise.why: A 7th arpeggio is the triad arpeggio you know with one more note, between the 5th and the next root, so learning where that one note sits finishes the shape.

cells.text:
The neck below shows the A minor arpeggio with one note added, the ringed {{b7}}. Press Play below to hear the arpeggio run up and back down, then play it yourself: start on the lowest {{1}}, play up to the highest note and come back down the same way.
Practice until your fingers pass through {{b7}} on the way to each {{1}} without stopping.

Two more 7th arpeggios from the same root. In A7, on the first neck below, the ringed {{3}} takes the place of the minor 3rd. In Amaj7, on the second, the ringed {{7}} sits one fret under each {{1}}.
Play each arpeggio up and back down, and say the name of the ringed note as you pass it.
Practice until you can name the ringed note before you reach it.

Press Play below to start the backing track at {{=bpm}}: Am7, D7, then two bars of Gmaj7, with the chords held under the notes. Play each arpeggio from the tab, one note per beat: up through the first three bars and down in the last.
Listen for the last note of the first two bars: it is the chord's 7th, and it sits one fret from a note of the chord that follows.
